utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we start the hearing, the Chamber would like to inform the parties that, pursuant to Rule 15 bis (A), today's hearing will take place in the absence of Judge Kinis. Judge Kinis is away for urgent personal reasons, and Judge Gwaunza and I have concluded that it is in the interests of justice to continue the trial of this hearing without Judge Kinis, who will be present again at next week's hearing. And, of course, Judge Kinis will read carefully the transcript of today's hearing. We scheduled the hearing today to receive further information in relation to the motion for restraining order against the Republic of Croatia, pursuant to Rule 54. And, again, before we start, Mr. Misetic, one filing in this context was ex parte, and as you may remember from the past in -- on an issue which has at least some relation to this one, there have been ex parte filings before. What is your suggestion as far as -- do we ask, do we go in closed session and send out all the parties or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the intention of the Chamber is with respect to the ex parte attachments. However, if it is going to be used in court and shown for any purpose, then, yes, I would ask that it remain ex parte from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- from the Prosecution only and not from the other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar reminds me that it is not that easy. We have to set up a whole new LiveNote if we go into any ex parte hearing. Now if just reference would be made to it and if it would not be shown, just reference to documents, without giving all the details of that, would that meet any objection as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, my intention is, Mr. President, if it is just reference to Mr. Ivanovic, that's fine. Other persons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say any other person --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if we are talking about a document on the which the name of Mr. Ivanovic appears and what type of document it is, for example, is it a letter, is it a -- is it -- well, whatever, that would not meet any objections as far as you're concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear. Then we will see how matters go. I'm informed that the delegation of the Republic of Croatia has arrived, and I would like them to be escorted into the courtroom. While awaiting their arrival, it is already on the record of yesterday that the accused have expressed their wish not to be present today, and they are not present in this courtroom. Good morning to the delegation of Croatia. This Chamber has invited the parties and the Republic of Croatia for this hearing which we may have some questions for you, and in which we would receive further information on an outstanding matter, the outstanding matter being the defendant Ante Gotovina's motion for a restraining order against the Republic of Croatia, pursuant to Rule 54. Could I first invite you to introduce yourself. We received a list, but, nevertheless, I would like it know who is who. The head of the delegation is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Gordan Markotic, head of the Department for cooperation with international Tribunals in the Ministry of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Josip Cule, deputy state attorney of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. POKUPEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zeljka Pokupec, the municipal state attorney in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the fourth member is Mr. Crncec, Ivan Crncec, head of the Department for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. He is dislocated sitting over there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers to kindly be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to come a bit closer to your microphones. There are three of you, so that's -- perhaps you could adjust the microphones in such a way that we can hear everything that you say. Mr. Misetic, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, just for purposes of the record, Mr. President, let me note that Mr. Marin Ivanovic is seated to my right this morning. Si in case the Chamber has any questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me to try to come to the core of this hearing straightaway. One of the issues raised by the Gotovina Defence is that the Republic of Croatia should not proceed against Mr. Ivanovic because Mr. Ivanovic, as is put by the Gotovina Defence, enjoys functional immunity. Now, this Chamber has received a letter by the Republic of Croatia sent to this Chamber, dated the 27th of April, 2009, where we read in the heading, Written arguments of the Republic of Croatia in connection with the request of indictee Ante Gotovina that the Republic of Croatia issues a court order forbidding certain procedures. Now, we find some information in it, but I could not find one word spent on the issue of immunity. Could you perhaps explain the position of the Republic of Croatia in relation to immunity? You have explained in the letter that you do not object to the way in which the Gotovina Defence seeks its evidence, that you do not impose any duty that it should be done through state channels. It seems that you agree on that. You have explained that the proceedings against Mr. Ivanovic are independent from the proceedings before this court, which, the Gotovina Defence deems irrelevant. You have explained that Croatia has a state interest in proceeding against Mr. Ivanovic, which, I would say, almost goes without saying, because if have you no interest in proceeding against a person, you wouldn't do it. But the whole issue, which seems to be the core issue here, has not been dealt with, and that is the claim by the Gotovina Defence that Mr. Ivanovic enjoys functional immunity. Could you explain the position of the Republic of Croatia in respect of what seems, to this Chamber, to be the core issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the question of immunity is used by -- is viewed by us through the prism of domestic rules and regulations, I would like to give the floor to the deputy state attorney, Mr. Cule, who is going to explain the issue of immunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, in the legislation of the Republic of Croatia, there are individual who is enjoy immunity. The question of immunity was resolved on the basis of a number of legal provisions based on the European conventions relating to diplomatic representatives and their circle. The other rules and regulations of those of the Republic of Croatia and as speak about the immunity enjoyed by the top leaders of executive power and authority, and all these rules and regulations, the Defence counsel, member of the Defence team which appear before foreign courts and also before courts in the Republic of Croatia do not enjoy any kind of immunity. As far as a separate law is concerned that we have in the Republic of Croatia, a specific law, it is the constitutional law on cooperation with International Criminal Courts, dated to 1996, in that law, the question of immunity is mentioned and also the circle of individuals enjoying immunity. According to Article 34 of that law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you to slow down because otherwise our interpreters have problems, and we would police part of your words which we'd rather not. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker kindly approach the microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, yes. I'm going to quote Article 34 of the law, constitutional law, that is, on cooperation with International Criminal Courts which says the Judges, Prosecutor, and Registrar of the International Criminal Court in the Republic of Croatia enjoy a special benefits and immunities provided for by the international right governing diplomatic representatives. So there legal provision does not provide for any kind of immunity for Defence counsel or members of the Defence teams. I should also like to add one more thing, and that is, that as far as we know, in criminal proceedings which have been initiated and are conducted in the Republic of Croatia, no -- none of the accused persons referred to their right to immunity or called upon their right to immunity. It is customary that if persons who stand accused consider that they have the right to enjoy immunity, then, they must refer to that right specifically and in that case, it is the competent court which will decide whether they in fact will enjoy that right or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. I immediately now address you, Mr. Misetic. From your submissions, it does not appear anywhere that immunity is invoked before the local court or local prosecutorial authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. We believe the issue is one of jurisdiction before this court and not the court or the authorities of the Republic of Croatia. We would state, for example, if an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor were to be charged, our response would be that I think it would be clear under Article 30 that that investigator would enjoy the immunities afforded to him under Article 30. The -- whether or not those immunities were granted under the Croatian constitutional law would be irrelevant under the statute. Those immunities would exist by virtue of a resolution of the Security Council, irrespective of any laws of the Republic of Croatia affirming that -- or recognizing the decision of the Security Council in passing the Statute. Secondly, I don't think there would be any issue that, for example, if the question of immunity of an OTP investigator in Zagreb were raised before a court in Zagreb, that that would preclude the Tribunal from taking any measures under Rule 54, nor -- and that would in effect concede that a court in Zagreb could find that a member of the Office of the Prosecutor didn't have immunity. That is a decision, I believe, that would be -- fall exclusively within the realm of the Tribunal to make the decision. And for that reason, we think that this is an issue that can be decided right now by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, just for argument's sake, if Mr. Ivanovic would have invoked immunity before the court and it would have been granted, it's just -- I'm not say it would, but let's just assume, then this whole exercise would have been superfluous, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it would be superfluous to seek -- quite frankly and speaking quite openly, to have sought immunity from a court in Zagreb is basically a waste of time because I think we all what the result of that would have been. There having been no precedent established yet by the Tribunal because the issue hasn't been decided, it would result essentially in needless delays, and ultimately this decision is going to wind up with the Chamber one way or the other. There are also, quite frankly, other considerations because the matter would essentially have to be referred to someone to consider whether there is immunity. When issues like this have arisen in the past -- and I will give you one example. When Mr. Rajcic was called to testify in the proceeding in Zagreb, he stated that he was precluded from testifying by some decision of this Chamber, if the Court will recall. What the judge in Zagreb did was did not decide the issue of whether there was any -- if you wish to call it immunity or prohibition on Mr. Rajcic, and the judge referred it to Mr. Markotic, who then referred back to you, essentially, to ask whether there is any impediment to seeking Mr. Rajcic's testimony in Zagreb. Essentially, that is the same thing that would happen here. We have cut the process short, and ask directly that the Chamber resolve the matter, because if we want to be realistic about what is going to happen this Zagreb, that is essentially what's going to happen because there is no decision yet at the international level resolving this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. You say we couldn't expect anything; therefore, we ask this Chamber to interfere in internal matters without even having tried to gain the -- what you consider to be the appropriate decision by a local court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't consider it an internal matter, first of all, Mr. President. I consider it a matter of this Tribunal. We are a Defence team not internally within the Republic of Croatia but internationally as part of this institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the proceedings are --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: They may be, indeed, domestic proceedings, but nevertheless, I am articulating what I believe the powers are of the Chamber under Rule 54. Now, to borrow a phrase of yours, Mr. President, if it's that we have to do a ritual dance of going through hoops and then getting our rejection from the authorities in Zagreb and then coming back to you within the next four months, obviously we will do that ritual dance. But I suspect that this issue is going to be back on the Chamber's plate at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. You have referred to domestic law, whereas, apparently, Mr. Misetic relies on international obligations under the Statute. Have you considered whether there are any obligations that derive from the Statute, which would prevail over or be inconsistent with or would contradict the position of the Republic of Croatia that Defence counsel have no immunity, no functional immunity?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to say that as far as we are concerned, the situation in the Republic of Croatia is clear. Our job is clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, might I interrupt. My colleague, while Mr. Cule was talking, it said Mr. Crncec and then Markotic. I would like to say for the record that everything that was said relating to immunity was Mr. Cule speaking. So could that be put right in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The record usually is revised at -- at the end of the day. There are -- quite understandable, there are always small inaccuracies, but it is good that you have drawn the attention to this inaccuracy. Yes, Mr. Cule, please proceed, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will proceed. It is the criminal section and crimes committed in the territory of the Republic of Croatia so the laws valid in Croatia are applied, both in material terms in other law -- procedural law. As far as trials before the International Criminal Courts are concerned, these laws are not applied in the Republic of Croatia. And I'd just like to mention that the question of application, that is to say, the application of the International Criminal Courts in a way has already been discussed before the International Criminal Court and the Chamber there which decided about what rules were to be applied in the case of the transfer of criminal proceedings or trials in the Ademi/Norac trial to local Courts. And in that case it was established that the legislation of the Republic of Croatia fully complies with all the standards and satisfies all standards of the domestic rules -- will be applied in those legal proceedings. When we turn towards domestic rules and regulations, all I can say is that -- All I can say is what I said at the beginning. And that is that domestic laws and rules and regulations do provide for the possibility of allowing Defence counsel or members of Defence teams to have functional immunity. And that is in conformity and consistent with the law governing criminal proceedings as well as the constitutional law on cooperation with International Criminal Tribunals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware that the legal advisor of the Secretary-General has delivered an opinion in relation to the Rwanda Tribunal, which clearly expresses that Defence counsel and staff employed by Defence counsel enjoy at least some kind of immunity?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we take a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This issue was raised. However, as immunity is concerned, that would have to be extended to encompass the commission of crimes committed in the territory of the Republic of Croatia during the period of the indictment. We are of the opinion that in such a case, such an extension could not be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're talking about the indictment, you're talking about the indictment brought against Mr. Ivanovic? Or any other indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The indictments raised against the accused Ivanovic, Sare, and Kretic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you say is if there's immunity, it does not apply to anything that happened on the territory of Croatia. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps a better formulation would be to say that it would be impossible to apply immunity in relation to crimes committed in the territory of the Republic of Croatia when people outside the circle I referred to previously are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say, Wherever they may have immunity, not on our territory. Let me then ask you the following question. Most of the job to be done in preparing for a Defence would have to be done on the territory of Croatia, isn't it? That is, finding witnesses, finding documentary materials, et cetera. Now, I understood that your argument would effectively deprive the Defence if they would have immunity, because that was the assumption starting point of your answer, whether you agree with that or not, it would be totally ineffective because the area where the job for which functional immunity, if it exists, should be done would be excluded from the scope of the functional immunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not believe that would be the right conclusion, given that Defence, in the territory of the Republic of Croatia can then take a whole spectrum of measures, whatever they deem necessary for the proceedings, but I do not believe that they should be allowed to commit crimes. If there was a crime committed, the state attorney's office, in keeping with the existing regulation, needs to prosecute the perpetrators of such crimes ex officio. The difference is that in that, that Defence has the right to undertake a number of measures that they find necessary without committing crimes, especially those crimes which are prosecuted ex officio. In that case, or in such a case the state prosecutor's office in keeping with the law is duty-bound to prosecute the perpetrators of such crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't there be, an international obligation to seek the immunity to be lifted, if it exists? And is that considered, which would open the way to a prosecution without a potential violation of any obligation to respect immunity? Again, it is for argument's sake. This Chamber, at this moment, does not express a view on whether immunity attaches to the function of Mr. Ivanovic. But just for argument's sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my introduction I said that according to the regulations in place in the Republic of Croatia, such persons do not enjoy immunity. Therefore, the state prosecutor's office was not duty-bound to deal with the issue of taking that immunity away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, would -- I have drawn your attention to the fact that at least the legal advisor of the Secretary-General -- when I say legal advisor, I think it's wrong; that's not exactly his position. But someone in the office for legal affairs within the headquarters of the United Nations, Mr. Johnson. He comes to a different conclusion, and if we look at -- for example, the agreement on the privileges and immunities of the International Criminal Court, there, clearly, we find rules on immunity for Defence counsel. And, of course, one of the arguments invoked by the Gotovina Defence is that it would be in line with Article 30 of the Statute of this Tribunal that Defence falls within the scope of Article 30. And we're talking about the Statute with this Security Council resolution. I take it that you have read the submissions made by the Gotovina Defence in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend Mr. Crncec will respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CRNCEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wanted to point out the fact that in keeping with the Article 30 of the Statute invoked by the Defence, which refers to the immunity of the members of Defence teams before International Criminal Tribunals and the ICTY, that is a different and separate legal argument in relation to the agreement on the privileges and immunities which applies to the ICC. Therefore, we believe the Statute of the ICTY is relevant in this specific case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the interpretation of legal instruments is often done in a comparative way as well. The Defence states that it is on the basis of an equality of arms that you can't give the Prosecution immunity and deprive Defence from such immunity. And they rely on an opinion, I would say, an opinion the ICTR has asked for, the president of the ICTR has asked for in a situation similar to the ICTY. So, therefore, it's a matter of interpretation of Article 30 and it's not uncommon that you then look over the borders and for purposes of interpreting Article 30 to see what opinions, authoritative opinions, have been produced and how the matter is dealt with in other international courts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you switch it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CRNCEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I do not wish to go into the interpretation of various decisions of the municipal court or the state attorney's office. It has to do with what my learned friend Mr. Cule said before, and that is that, under the constitutional law which has to do with the -- with cooperation with the ICTY, we incorporated the provisions of Article 30 in that law, in keeping with the provision 34 of our constitutional law and Article 30 of the ICTY Statute, before Croatian national courts, including the municipal court in Zagreb, the issue of immunity was not raised. The state -- the municipal state attorney's office was not duty-bound to do that ex officio. I believe that is the core of the issue. We followed the letter of the constitutional law, the Statute, under which the Defence does not enjoy immunity. None of them raise that issue before the municipal court. The state prosecutor's office was not duty-bound to act ex officio. Therefore, before the municipal court in Zagreb, that issue was not raised at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say, We never even came to a legal debate on whether immunity would apply or not because the matter was not raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. CRNCEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I respond to that point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I wish to, perhaps I failed to state earlier, to not confuse two points. Mr. Ivanovic raising the issue of immunity in his -- in the courts in Zagreb, first and foremost would presuppose that wee would have to exhaust the legal remedies in the Republic of Croatia or he would have to exhaust those remedies. If the Court in Zagreb were to take weeks, months, et cetera, to resolve the issue, then that delay would continue. Would he have to appeal the decision to a higher court in the Republic of Croatia, at what point would Mr. Ivanovic -- I should say would the issue be raised with the Trial Chamber? The issue I wish to reiterate is the issue before this Chamber is not Marin Ivanovic per se; it's Ante Gotovina. The issues here concern Ante Gotovina's fundamental rights under Article 21 to equality of arms, and it is this Court's primary jurisdiction to protect Ante Gotovina's fundamental rights and to issue all orders that are necessary to do that. The Courts of the Republic of Croatia are not charged with resolving the issue of whether Ante Gotovina has a fundamental right to equality of arms under Article 21 of the Statute. So we would disagree with the interpretation of the Republic of Croatia. That protection of Ante Gotovina's rights under Article 21 under -- is specifically entrusted to the Trial Chamber under Article 20 of the Statute, and the issue of Mr. Ivanovic is not an issue of Mr. Ivanovic's personal immunity. It is whether Ante Gotovina's Defence team has immunity, such that it can in its functions and obligations to both Mr. Gotovina and this Court, can function appropriately. The delay inherent in asking a court in Croatia which does not have jurisdiction over Ante Gotovina or his rights would cause continuing damage to Ante Gotovina in the course of these proceedings. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Is there anything more at this moment to be said about the substance of immunity beyond what was already submitted in writing? Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: On the issue of just -- on the question of immunity. Just to follow up one point. I don't know if it was clear and I don't know -- I may have misunderstood the arguments advanced by Croatia, so if I have, I apologise in advance. But, I believe, as a general statement, it was stated that Defence counsel do not enjoy immunity as a broad statement, not just ICTY. And as the Court is aware, Defence counsel at the ICC are immune from Prosecution or process, I should say, on the territory of the Republic of Croatia pursuant to an agreement reached between the Republic of Croatia and the ICC in 2003. So the issue is not whether Croatian laws as a blanket matter do not provide immunity for international Defence counsel. It is now simply whether ICTY Defence counsel enjoy that immunity, because ICC Defence counsel already do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the term "immunity" seems to be a rather complex legal concept. Just for my information, if counsel would be called as a witness, would he be under an obligation to testify about matters that he confidentially discussed with any of his clients?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He would not, given that counsel of an accused is part of the circle of persons who, under the law on criminal procedure, are free from providing testimony, in terms of attorney/client privilege. In that case, if such a person were to be called as a witness, could invoke the immunity he or she enjoys as part of his role as Defence counsel. That is expressly stated in one of the provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Search and seizures in law firms, is there any prohibition in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult for me to follow the thrust of your question. But if an attorney also acts as Defence counsel, there are certain regulations in keeping with the law of Republic of Croatia in which it is regulated now any searches and seizures can be conducted of an attorney's office or the contents of his case. Such a search is not allowed in terms of documents. That would constitute illegal -- illegally gained proof, and any judgement could not be based on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that it is in dispute whether or not the Prosecution has any standing in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I just wish to make a point on the last point if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would first do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is one of the fundamental issues of this motion, generally speaking, Mr. President. For the record the Republic of Croatia is compelling police interviews of virtually every member of the Gotovina Defence as we speak in Zagreb to go to police stations and give compulsory police interviews. So this is not a theoretical question, it's a real question. I have very little ability to control what a person in our office may or may not reveal in the course of a conversation in a police station. Those reports are being given to the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Ivanovic is an attorney in Zagreb and was compelled to give a police interview in March, which is now appended to a Prosecution filing. So these issues are not simply theoretical. For the record we object to them as violations of Rule 70 and Rule 97, and we have continually expressed to the Republic of Croatia that its continuing insistence on interviewing through police measures and members of the Defence is a violation of the rules of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I first seek verification of what you just told us. You say it is not just that Mr. Ivanovic is proceeded against at this moment, but there are compulsory police interviews with more members of your team. Could I first seek verification whether that is the case or not? And, Mr. Misetic, could you give us an indication as to how many. Would that be two, three?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge ... it's at least five and counting, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least five and counting. Could I ask you, Mr. Cule, to -- yes, if you would activate your microphone, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and be clear. In a case when there are criminal -- when there is criminal processing or investigation, the police does have the right to call in citizens to provide them with information. The citizen is duty-bound to respond to the police invitation. They are not duty-bound to answer questions, and the police does not have the right to re-call him with respect to the same crime that he might possibly be charged with, nor is the citizen duty-bound to respond to any additional calls from the police. So that can't be the case. It can't be forcible interviews which are repeated in such a way as to force a person to come in and place him in a detrimental position of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first try to establish. Are they called for interviews as suspects of crime, or are they called as potential witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are called into these interviews not as suspects. If they were called as suspects, then that would be state in the summons; they are summoned as citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is, that they are summoned so they have to appear, and they will be interviewed not because there is a factual basis for a suspicion that they would have committed a crime, but because they apparently have knowledge which is of interest for ongoing proceedings or ongoing investigations against others. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. They needn't be proceedings against other individuals. There can be suspicion that a crime has been committed and that those individuals have certain knowledge. So a statement is taken from them if they wish to give it. And that statement, as a rule, will be sent to the state attorney's office in question, and it will be up to them to decide whether to take the case further or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then seek a further clarification of part of your answer. You said, and I'm reading from page 20, lines 4 and following: "They are not duty-bound to answer questions, and the police does not have the right to re-call him with respect to the same crime that he might possibly be charged with ..." Which language strongly suggests that the interview relates to a matter for where -- for which the person that is interviewed will be charged with, which puts him in a position pretty close to a suspect. I'm quoting your words, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. When I said in my introduction and referred to what Mr. Misetic said, I spoke about the position of a suspect, and after that, I went on to speak about what happens when citizens are called in for interviews. I understood your first question to be what the procedure was towards suspects. And so what I said at the -- in the introduction is the right of a suspect. That's how we treat it. We look at the rights of suspects in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic, you would like to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, persons on our Defence team have been called more than once to police interviews, so I'm not sure where the distinction is between our position and the Croatian position is. Mr. Ivanovic, even after he was indicted, was called back for a compulsory police interview which is now attached to an OTP filing. That's the first point. The second is that the Republic of Croatia states that these interviews are in relation to a crime. One of the persons that was interviewed from our office -- one of the persons that was interviewed from our office who, before we knew that they had been called to a police interview, was called into the police station and asked questions such as, Who works in the office; who has what responsibilities within the Gotovina Defence team; how do you communicate with each other; internal workings of the Gotovina Defence which don't seem to be related to any specific document, et cetera. Those then are then being put together in reports. I'm unaware whether internal workings of the Gotovina Defence have been disclosed or are to be disclosed to the Office of the Prosecutor in this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask. Again, I said I'm seeking verification of what Mr. Misetic tells us, that several members, on a first counting five, were compulsorily interviewed by the police. First of all, apart from your general statement on what the powers, and what of the police, and what duties of citizens are, is it correct that several persons from the Gotovina Defence team have been called for interviews where they had to appear?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission I would just like to explain something that is very -- that is vital to these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... explain anything, but I'd first like to have an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the question is linked to precisely the response that my colleague wished to make, Mr. Markotic wished to make, and it is this. He is going to try and explain why these individuals were called in the first place because it wasn't a question of just criminal proceedings. There was something beyond a criminal procedure that was, in part, linked to the Ministry of the Interior, and that is the portion that Mr. Markotic wishes to explain to you and how these people were called in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just was verifying whether they were called and the number. And then the next question, and suggested by Mr. Markotic is to explain why they were called. But let's first try to keep to the facts. Were some five members of the team called by the police? And let's not start struggling over four or six, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to put it this way. The municipal state attorney's office, after it received a report from the Ministry of Justice on an administrative investigation, asked for information from the police and criminal processing. At this point in time I can't say with any degree of certainty how many people were called by the Ministry of Internal Affairs, that is to say, the police called for those interviews. However, those individuals were not called only because of the interest shown in criminal processing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it seems to be a problem. Just as a first step to establish whether persons were called, and even if you do not know the precise number, which I understand -- were persons called? That's the first question. And then I will ask you why they were called, but I'd like to do it step by step. Were persons called by the police for interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some persons, quite certainly, were called in order to perform an inquiry, to conduct an inquiry. For the needs of a potential criminal procedure. And that's what I want to stress because of possible criminal proceedings later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... opportunity to explain whatever you want to explain at a later stage. But I first want to the have the factual information. So persons were called. You do not know exactly the number of persons called. At the same time, you do not say it's impossible that there were five, as Mr. Misetic tells us. Second question: Those persons, were they under a duty to come? I'm not yet asking whether they were under a duty to answer, but were they under an obligation to appear for such an interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Zeljka Pokupec will answer that question because she is the municipal state attorney in Zagreb, and she is better versed in the matter and the procedure taken by the police, pursuant to the municipal state attorney's instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. POKUPEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, after the municipal state attorney's office in Zagreb received a report from the Administration and Department for Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal of the Ministry of Justice which represents the criminal report as well indicates the existence of possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm really going to stop you. I said again and again that you have an opportunity to explain whatever you want to explain, but I first want the facts. The facts, we have now established, that a number of people were called by the police. My next question was, Were they under an obligation to come?

utterances.speaker: MS. POKUPEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Third --

utterances.speaker: MS. POKUPEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of people were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That being established, I follow up first, because what I'm doing, I'm verifying, at this moment, whether what Mr. Misetic tell us, whether there is any dispute about that. Then later if you say, But this should be understood in a certain context, I will give you an opportunity to do so. One of the things that was put by Mr. Misetic, that the results of such interviews, the content of it, were given to the Office of the Prosecution in The Hague. I just want to establish whether that happened or not. Whether they were good reasons for it is different matter, but I just first want to establish what the facts are. Was the content, or any report on such interviews, was that relayed to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. POKUPEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So from the criminal proceedings reports were relayed about raising indictments against Marin Ivanovic and Jurica Sare and Marijan Kretic. And it wasn't an information interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you whether the information which was relayed to the Office of the Prosecution, did it deal with any internal matters of the Gotovina Defence? The internal working of the internal organisation, the division of tasks? Because I'm verifying point by point, whether, what Mr. Misetic tells us, whether there is any factual merit in it. If you don't know, tell us; if you do know, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. POKUPEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the organisation goes, we did not have that information, and that information did in the go to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic told us that these were the questions. You now tell us that you didn't have that information. There are several options, one of them being that the questions were not answered. Were questions put to those persons who were called for an interview in relation to the internal dealings of the Gotovina Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The state attorney's office, with respect to these circumstances, did not ask to have an interview with them. We did not receive that information, and we did not pass it on to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was whether questions were asked in that respect. Because we had established -- you told us already that you didn't have the information. And information you don't have, you can't pass to anyone else. But then my next question was whether questions were asked in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I did not have an opportunity to explain why the police could have talked in another way to these individuals. Because that is the part which relates to the administrative inquiry and investigation. And within that part, possibly that kind of question was asked, but the state attorney's office cannot know about that. Possibly, in what the police undertook, it did ask those questions, possibly. But I or, rather, the state attorney's office cannot know about that on the basis of any records or interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is quite simple and, don't worry, this courtroom is reserved until a quarter to 2.00, so don't worry about that you don't have an opportunity to explain. But, again, I want to clearly distinguish between facts and positions taken in respect of those facts. It's of no use to discuss the why is -- if the question of whether it happened and -- has not been answered. I want to have a clear factual basis. I want to know exactly where there's any dispute about the facts to start with. So you say, I do not know. Such questions may have been put to those persons. Mr. Misetic, is there any other factual matter which I should address at this moment? I think that we went through the most important ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I can state as a fact that in fact the MUP did conduct such interviews, posed those questions, the person from our office I did not have time to instruct on Rule 70 and Rule 97, and then that person did answer in detail the questions that were put to him. Subsequent people are being called in. We have managed to instruct subsequent people to invoke Rule 70 and Rule 97 to which the police respond, It doesn't matter; we have already learned everything anyway about how you all work inside the office. So I think that matter should be -- not be in dispute. I trust what my colleagues from the state attorney's office state, that they don't have that information, but it is certain that it is in the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Having verified the facts, I would now like to give you an opportunity to explain, as you apparently wish to do, and I'm carefully listening to you why the interviews were conducted and what we should know about them more, in order to understand the position of the Croatian government. Mr. Markotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to remind you of a fact which in fact was the reason for which the whole inquiry was undertaken and that -- the fact that people were interviewed. In May 2007, the Prosecution of the ICTY asked that a subpoena be issued against Croatia for them to provide the lacking materials from the special police and the Ministry of Defence, the so-called artillery logs and documentation. Now in July of last year, we appeared before this Trial Chamber. And on the 16th of September, 2008, we received instructions from the Court that we will to expand and intensify the investigation in order to find the documents that were still lacking and that were being sought by the Prosecution and requested by the Prosecution, and to provide all the documents we come up with during our investigation and the sources from which those documents were sourced. The names and functions of the individuals who were interviewed during these proceedings and to provide transcripts of those interviews. In carrying out the decision taken by the Trial Chamber, we did indeed carry out interviews. We conducted interviews as far as military documents were concerned, and we interviewed about 113 individuals relating to military aspects. To police documents, we interviewed 130 persons. And they are the official reports that were provided both to the Tribunal and to the OTP in keeping with the instructions given by the Trial Chamber on the 16th of September, 2008. In those interviews, people were mostly asked about those documents that were still lacking and following list C of the Prosecution provided with the subpoena issued against Croatia for that purpose. So that is the administrative investigation inquiry conducted by the Ministry of Justice, the Ministry of Defence, and the Ministry of Interior, in order to arrive at the facts to see where those lacking documents were. After all this was done, and we sent the OTP and the Tribunal five reports with annexes and appendices about everything that we did, we also tabled a report to the state attorney's office, which ex officio then, as the report contained elements of a criminal report under Croatian law to initiate criminal proceedings against these three individuals that were mentioned. I, myself, do not have any knowledge, nor do I know whether in those official reports the structure of the work of the Defence teams was asked about. Because, first of all -- the prime object was to come up with the documents that were lacking and which we were asked to find by the Tribunal and to then pass on. So, along with all the other relevant facts and everything else we did within the frameworks of this administrative investigation, that was the basis and foundations upon which the state attorney's office launched criminal proceedings. And the same reports were sent on to this Trial Chamber and to the OTP of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you then one question. I do understand that Mr. Ivanovic is charged for concealing or destroying of two documents. Were these among the documents that were asked for by the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. POKUPEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this specific case, the documents that are included in the indictment against Marin Ivanovic, it is not certain whether these were the documents sought by the OTP of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It is unimportant, rather than not certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. POKUPEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents were supposed to be contained in the archives of the Republic of Croatia and the concealment of such documents represents a crime which is prosecuted ex officio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you, then, although the order was issued by the Chamber, and the Chamber in September very much insisted on further investigations. Apparently you have interviewed members of the Gotovina Defence team. The Chamber knows that a lot of documents were received. In the proceedings before this Tribunal, the Chamber does not start studying all of them because we wait, we give them to the parties, and we wait and see whether they want to present these documents as evidence before the Chamber. Now -- so, therefore, this Chamber is not privy of the contents of those documents. The parties most likely are. Now, have any of the documents sent since September, because the earlier reports were that you'd given all that was available. Then -- but that was not all that was sought. We then invited you to intensify your searches. Have the -- has any document ever been retrieved from members of the Defence team or through the information provided during these interviews with members of the Defence team? So I'm trying to find out what -- where we have received quite a number of documents of which the content is not -- which -- with which I'm not acquainted, whether, to say so, the Defence team of Mr. Gotovina has been a source of additional documents and information which was subsequently provided to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. CRNCEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the answer is yes. Some documents were received by -- from the Defence or information gained through interviews conducted can Defence team members. In the opinion -- in the opinion of the Croatian military experts, such documents do fall under the category of the documents included in the OTP request, in terms of the 54 bis proceedings. That is to say, Croatia is duty-bound to provide such documents in keeping with the September order of this Court. In order to respond to your previous question, concerning the two documents contained in the indictment against Mr. Ivanovic, in terms of the information we have for the time being, they are not included in that category of documents. It is a personal diary for which our military analysts believed would be included. It is a -- they thought it was a working diary of the Artillery Group number 5. But as far as I know, both Defence and the Prosecution expressed their view that such a document is not included in the group. The other document is a map, which is not among the artillery logs sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I want to leave now the area, again, of the substance of interviews and -- because this Chamber, at least at this moment in time, has not sufficient information to form an opinion about the substance, and it is even the question whether the Chamber should form any opinion about that. It is only because Mr. Misetic raised, that the case brought against Mr. Ivanovic is part of, if I could say it, short, wider operation, that I briefly inquired into what had happened and why that happened. I would like to leave that area at this moment. As far as immunity until now is concerned, and I'm addressing you, Mr. Tieger, knowing that Mr. Misetic is of the opinion that you have no standing in this matter, but I nevertheless invite you to make any additional submissions, if you wish to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just clarify our position, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I believe I stated, or I should have stated, is there has been no articulated position of standing by the Prosecution. That doesn't mean that they don't or can't articulate a position, but what we also suggested in our reply was that more along the lines consistent with what we have just heard now, which is that this case is connected to an overall -- has a relationship to the Trial Chamber's order of the 16th of September, and if that is the case, then that's the Prosecution's argument, I suppose, for standing in this Chamber. But that should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The parties have invoked both a lack of standing, Mr. Gotovina issued has no -- has a lack of standing in relation to Mr. Ivanovic. You said at least not an articulated standing for the Prosecution. It may be clear that the issue could possibly affect the position of the parties, I would say, as far as Mr. Tieger is concerned, that if there are any concerns, that these investigations are needed in order to fully meet what the Chamber asked the Croatian government to do. I'm not saying that this is the proper way to do it, whether there are any limits to that is a different question. But just to say that it could affect the position of the Prosecution, just as I would say the proceedings against Mr. Ivanovic could have an impact on the position of Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I actually agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I wish to reiterate is that that should be stated because there has been a argument advanced that what is happening in Zagreb -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should have been stated. I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... No, no, no, but let me explain why I say that. There is an argument before the Chamber, arguing to, both from the Prosecution and the Republic of Croatia, arguing that you should deny the motion because it is interference in the domestic matters of the Republic of Croatia. If in fact, as you articulate, the situation is that this is part of a proceeding for which the Prosecution has standing because it relates to a matter pending before the Tribunal, then is not strictly a domestic issue of the Republic of Croatia. And that is why I asked that that be articulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear. Now, whether it has any impact, sometimes internal matters can have an impact on other matter but still remain in the domain of the domestic authorities. I'm not saying that this is such a case, but the mere fact that a development has an impact on this Tribunal does not automatically - and I emphasise automatically - mean that the Tribunal has the authority and the power to intervene. But I just was about to establish that this -- these developments may have an impact on the position of both parties. If not, I think we would not even have had this hearing. Mr. Tieger, any -- Mr. Russo?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. We won't address the specific issue of standing unless the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it seems not to be a major issue anymore, unless you want to address only the standing of Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I'd much prefer to stick to the issues which have been raised during the hearing today with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, from the fact that I invite you to make any further submissions from the fact that Mr. Misetic said, Well, it has not been explained properly perhaps, but I do not as such. Let's go to the substance of the matter. If there's anything on the -- on the functional immunity that you would like to add beyond what has been submitted in writing and what was said today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Thank you, Mr. President. We clearly did not address the issue of forum shopping in our response, because we hear for the first time today that Mr. Ivanovic has not invoked immunity before the courts in Croatia. Our position with respect to that is that this is an improper attempt to forum shop the issue of immunity to this court rather than a court before which it belongings. Now whether Mr. Ivanovic enjoys immunity, of course, is a separate issue from who decides whether or not Mr. Ivanovic enjoys immunity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will come to that. I will come to that. You mean which court or even further which administrative authority within this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will deal with that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic ties the issue of forum shopping, in other words he tells this Trial Chamber, I'm coming to you because it is a waste of time to speak to the courts in Croatia. That, I would argue to the Trial Chamber, is simply an admission of the fact that he is forum shopping this issue. But irrespective of that, he seems to be relying on the position of the prosecuting authority with respect to immunity and no one has, as yet, asked the court in Croatia whether it believes that immunity applies. If the Prosecutor takes a position opposed to that of the Defence, that is certainly nothing new in litigation. It would certainly not be appropriate if, for example, Mr. Misetic said, Well, the Prosecution believes Mr. Gotovina is guilty before the ICTY; it's a complete waste of time to ask Orie or any of the other Judges their opinion with respect to that; I'm going to go directly to the European Court of Human Rights to get just for my client. It's simply not the forum in which it should be done. Whether it would cause delay in this proceeding is a red-herring issue, Mr. President. Any procedure by which the issue of immunity will be resolved will necessarily involve some form of delay. That, of course, is tied back to who determines whether there is in fact immunity and who determines whether such immunity will be waived and under what circumstances. If this court were to decide to take up the issue, the Court would have to make factual findings, determine exactly what happened. There's no reason why this court needs to do it, as opposed to another court or an administrative body. But, in any case, asking the Court to intervene because of time considerations is an incredibly intrusive act by the Tribunal which delay can be addressed, for example, if the Gotovina Defence wanted to make an argument that this proceeding should be stayed or adjourned until such time as the immunity issue is resolved in another forum, that would address the concern of any impact that the collateral prosecution would have on the ability of Mr. Ivanovic or anyone else to assist in Mr. Gotovina's Defence. I would like to tie that also, Mr. President, to the fact that the relief being sought by the Gotovina Defence is not simply related to Mr. Ivanovic. They're seeking for the Trial Chamber to enjoin, not only the Prosecution of Mr. Ivanovic, but to enjoin even the investigation by prosecuting authorities in the government of Croatia into anyone who commits acts which the Gotovina Defence believes is in furtherance of its obligations before this Tribunal. There are obviously very serious considerations for this Chamber if it were to enter such an order. With respect to the issue of whether this is actually having any affect on Mr. Gotovina's preparations or presentation of his Defence, there has been no information provided on that whatsoever. There is merely the bold statement that this is -- has a chilling effect on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you're going beyond what I invited you to address. That is the immunity issue. Functional immunity. You're now talking about the effect, and I would first focus on the immunity issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One minute, and then we have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Russo is incorrect. We are not forum shopping. As I indicated there is only one authority for jurisdiction to protect Ante Gotovina's rights. Mr. Ivanovic' immunity is derivative of Ante Gotovina's rights under Article 21 of the statue, which would then flow into Article 30 of the statute. A court in Zagreb has no jurisdiction, and administrative body of the United Nations has no jurisdiction to protect the fundamental rights of Ante Gotovina under Article 21 of the Statute. And specifically Article 20 of the Statute authorises this Trial Chamber to protect Ante Gotovina's fundamental rights and to issue all such orders as are necessary to protect those rights. The issues here are equality of arms. And for that reason, Mr. President, we dispute the Prosecution's assertion and state that there can be no forum shopping when there is only one forum. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. We will have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I have a question for you, in relation to the time. You have submitted an, as you call it, accreditation letter, which dates from March 2008, I think, which refers to a request for accreditation on the -- I think it was on the 6th of March, but March 2008. Apart from whether the letter itself calls it registration rather than accreditation, at the same time, and I'm now quoting from the ex parte material, there Mr. Ivanovic appears on the list from 2006. That raises some questions as to if there's any immunity from when on it attaches. Could you give me your position in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, our position is that it attaches from the time that Mr. Ivanovic is recognised by the Republic of Croatia as working for the Gotovina Defence, and in the interests of the Gotovina Defence, within the Republic of Croatia. In other words, when they receive notice that he is acting in the capacity as a member of the Gotovina Defence. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may just complete that thought. What we had done in our filings, was to alert when the Trial Chamber was initially notified of Mr. Ivanovic's role on the team, which is I believe the 24th of July, 2006. The Registry -- what we had sent initially was, I believe, the -- and I'm not familiar necessarily with the precisely terminology, but whether it is accreditation or registration, it was on the eve of trial so that Mr. Ivanovic could appear in court and use e-court and those facilities that are necessary for participation from within the courtroom, which was then extended to him. But the Chamber, itself, has been on notice since the 24th of July, 2006. The Republic of Croatia has been on notice since very early in 2006, and we are in the process now of trying to retrieve a document or correspondence between the Republic of Croatia and Mr. Ivanovic. We can advise the Court that in the ordinary process of obtaining documents from the institutions of the Republic of Croatia, for example, from the state archive, our investigators will make the selections in the state archive. Typically then, the Croatian government will review those documents and then, when they are ready, they will be delivered to Mr. Ivanovic under cover letter in which it is indicated that the delivery of state documents to Mr. Ivanovic is being given purpose to the needs of the Defence before this Tribunal. So there should be very little, if any, dispute that the Republic of Croatia has known almost from the beginning of the proceedings before this Tribunal -- I should say from the formation of the Trial Chamber in this case that Mr. Ivanovic is employed by General Gotovina for purposes of his Defence. And in fact Mr. Ivanovic is one of the few -- I believe there is also one other attorney in Zagreb who may receive documents from the Republic of Croatia, but certainly most of the communication within Croatia between the Gotovina Defence and the Republic of Croatia has taken place between Mr. Ivanovic and/or our colleague, Mr. Fartic [phoen], and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you are referring to the 24th of July, did you mean - let me just see, 24th of June, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you look at our filing, Mr. President, in a footnote I indicated that when I sent the letter, I misdated it. And so it says the 24th of June, but it should be the 24th of July. And the Chamber will note that that was sent pursuant to an order of the Trial Chamber that was issued on the 14th of July, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is -- I missed that correction, as far as the date is concerned. Now, it is your position that whomever is on your team, if you give notice that immunity attaches, whether it is it Saint Joan of Arc or Al Capone, doesn't make any difference. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This goes into the issue of functional immunity. If there is notice to the government of Croatia that someone is acting in their capacity as a member of the Defence team, then acts which are conducted pursuant to the function of a member of the Defence team enjoy immunity. Al Capone would still be subject to the jurisdiction, if he were Croatian, of the Republic of Croatia for whatever other matters the Republic of Croatia may have an interest in prosecuting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if -- let's just assume, for argument sake, if a crime would be committed, you would say that person enjoys immunity until it is lifted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would, Mr. President. And I would note from the earlier submission of the Republic of Croatia, that in writing Croatia acknowledges the Blaskic Appeals Chamber decision and says that Croatia does not dispute that the Defence does not have to go through official channels to collect documents. But later on they say Croatia also has a right to prosecute crime, which, of course, leads us to the question of if the act is the collection of evidence which Croatia doesn't dispute does not need to go through official channels, but the taking of evidence without going through official channels is a crime, then we would suggest that that, per se, would fall within functional immunity. In other words if Croatia acknowledges that there is no obligation to go deliver documents first to the Republic of Croatia, then the act of retrieving documents for purposes of these proceedings should enjoy functional immunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if -- again, for argument's sake, if you would steal evidentiary material, you know that your neighbour has some relevant evidence, he doesn't want to give breaking and entering. How would you look at that? That is a -- certainly an activity which falls within the scope of preparing a Defence, but, at the same time, could be considered a commission of a crime. What in your view should be done under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In my view, Mr. President, the first step would be what has taken place frequently in this case, which is a communication from, for example, Mr. Markotic's office to the Trial Chamber of those allegations and a request that, on the basis of those allegations, either a further investigation take place or be allowed under the Trial Chamber's ruling, or otherwise a full lifting, if warranted, of the functional immunity. If in fact a Defence person was engaging in untoward methodology or methods of obtaining evidence, then obviously that is something that the Trial Chamber could continue to monitor, and Croatia or any other state would, of course, have the ability to petition the Chamber. I would note that, for example, if we were talking about the ICC, I think a similar procedure would take place where if a Defence attorney or investigator would engage in such conduct, what would be the recourse? Or to put it a different way, for purposes of this Tribunal, we, for example, I'll use myself, enjoy immunity here within the Netherlands under the headquarters agreement. If there was some relevant evidence located within the Netherlands, and I broke into and entered a facility in the Netherlands, I have immunity theoretically under the headquarters agreement. That doesn't preclude the Netherlands from petitioning the relevant -- I don't recall specifically the moment under the headquarters agreement who is to be petitioned, whether it is the President or the Secretary-General or a Trial Chamber, but nevertheless that is the procedure that would be employed, and I think a similar procedure should be employed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that immunity, in diplomatic circles is often resolved by sending the diplomat back and expecting that his home country would take appropriate action. Now, could you tell us now -- and I'll later ask the same question to you. Mr. Ivanovic can be considered to be both, in terms of diplomatic language, to be on mission in Croatia because that is where he performs his duties. That's just -- that's not an offence. Perhaps we could start administrative proceedings and inquiring and what happens. So often the solution is that a country which has jurisdiction takes over, that's usually the home country, but here we are in a situation where Mr. Ivanovic is both on mission and, from what I understand, to be fully transparent, you referred in one of your footnotes to the, I think to the -- what do they call it, the check in/check out march material. I had a look at that, because I had no idea what it was about, and then I noticed that the paperwork in relation to taking up residence in the Netherlands was all empty, which -- but I'm asking you, leads me to conclude that Mr. Ivanovic has not applied for residence in the Netherlands, or is still a resident of Croatia? We could ask Mr. Ivanovic, but I was unfamiliar with that, so I asked to see such a form, and then the Registry gave me the specific one for Mr. Ivanovic. I want to be very clear on that. And I noticed that all the forms about application for residence in the Netherlands, resident's permit, et cetera, were not -- these forms were all empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that Mr. Ivanovic has no residence in Netherlands, has residence in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you will understand what my question is, that whereas often the country of the state where someone enjoys immunity just doesn't take any action, but, of course, the territorial scope of the immunity is limited to the state where someone is accredited, whether or not this is accreditation or just registration is also perhaps a matter. But what, in your view, should be the -- apart from waiving the immunity, would there be any other solution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not -- I have to acknowledge, I'm not sure what the -- if you could advise me what is the specific problem that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if I have a diplomate, if I have a Belgian diplomate who is accredited in Germany, if he does something in Germany, they just expel him, they take him -- they withdraw his accreditation. He goes back to Belgium and, of course, Belgium could usually take appropriate criminal proceedings against that person, on the basis of the principle of active personality or also called a nationality principle. So there have you a fallback situation where the sending state would take appropriate measures. Whereas the sending state here, apparently is the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sending him to a -- or at least he performs his duties on the territory of Croatia, he has his residence on the territory of Croatia and, of course, the Tribunal has no power, no competence, to -- well, let's just assume that he would have committed a crime, to prosecute that in any way. Is there any other way than to seek the immunity to be waived?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me answer in two parts. First, ironically enough, I thought about this question but only actually in relation to you, in passing, which is what happens if a Dutch judge is appointed to the ICTY and has full diplomatic immunity, what does the Netherlands do in that situation? Unfortunately for me, I left it at that thought and never researched it further, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You better now understand why the question came into my mind, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I do. I guess it depends on the nature of the criminal offence, Mr. President. If we're talking about a criminal offence that arises from conduct -- in other words, from the function --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Breaking and entering to obtain evidence. Let's take that example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. The first thing delving deep in theory that comes to mind is, indeed, that also might be something that is certainly subject to a variety of measures that could be taken by the Tribunal itself. The first thing, as I'm aware, under Article 34 of the Code of Professional Conduct, we as Defence counsel are responsible for our staff, and so there are disciplinary measures within the Code of Professional Conduct that could be taken for such, what could be deemed misconduct. In other words engaging in activity that is untoward, not fair, and otherwise could be deemed as misconduct. The second issue is, of course, a question of whether there is a Rule 77 issue, and that could be construed as an interference with the administration of justice. So in terms of the Tribunal's jurisdiction to monitor the situation, there are those avenues. Outside of that, if we're talking about crime per se, and somebody committing a crime that is more than just a classification of an activity that is otherwise conducted in the normal course of preparing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Breaking and entering to obtain evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I -- indeed, at the present time no other remedy comes to mind other than to advise the Trial Chamber that such a conduct has occurred and to request that the person be subject to -- be relieved of the functional immunity for that act and to be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to put the same question to you. What, in your view, all on the basis of assuming that there would be immunity. I'm not expressing any view on that, but that is the basis on which the motion has been brought, and we are trying to understand it in all details. Therefore, we started with immunity. But now, on the basis of the assumption that there would be immunity, what, in your view, if under international law, under the Statute that would be an obligation to observe the immunity of staff members of a Defence team, what would the appropriate solution, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about a hypothetical situation, of course. And what is vital to that hypothetical situation is precisely the example that you quoted, Your Honour. In the specific case, we would have a citizen of his own country who, on the territory of his own country is trying to protect himself by invoking immunity from crime. Now, if we were to allow him, for example, and I'm talking about this as an example, if he were to steal archive material from an archive and the country of origin has to be informed -- has to inform a body outside the domestic jurisdiction to stop him, then this would provide this individual with the go-ahead to commit crimes unimpeded in future. So here we're dealing with a citizen that does not enjoy diplomatic immunity in a foreign state, in a foreign country. And even if he did have immunity, he would not have immunity in his own country. And bearing this in mind, if I might be allowed to finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CULE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And bearing in mind the development of the situation as we have had in the Republic of Croatia, and the circumstances under which this occurred, we consider that we can apply the provisions, legal provisions that apply in the Republic of Croatia and prosecute that individual. I see no other options. Faced with this situation, of course, I'm not an expert in these very subtle issued of immunity as seen by international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, two questions in this respect. We talked about the territorial scope sometimes of immunity.
